lessons.title: The ICT Foundation — Thinking Like an Institution
lessons.subtitle: Core Philosophy, IPDA, and the Algorithmic Market

steps.text: ICT methodology is built on the premise that financial markets are not random but follow predictable algorithms designed by institutions and central banks. Unlike retail traders who rely on lagging indicators and emotional decision-making, ICT teaches you to think like the institutions that actually move price.

The core philosophy is that price moves between liquidity pools, and understanding this flow allows you to predict where price is going next. Retail traders typically lose because they buy when institutions are selling and sell when institutions are buying.

ICT flips this paradigm by teaching you to trade alongside the smart money rather than against it. Every concept in ICT builds on this foundational shift in perspective from retail to institutional thinking.

The Interbank Price Delivery Algorithm (IPDA) is the mechanism that central banks and large financial institutions use to distribute price across the market. IPDA operates on a simple principle: accumulate liquidity in one area, then deliver price to the opposite area where opposing liquidity sits.

Think of IPDA as the engine that drives price from one liquidity pool to the next. It is the reason why markets make specific patterns that repeat across all timeframes and all instruments. Understanding IPDA means understanding that every price move has a purpose to hunt liquidity.
Stops cluster predictably around obvious highs and lows so sweeps occur often — but not every swing is engineered.

Modern financial markets are dominated by algorithmic trading systems operated by the largest banks and hedge funds. These algorithms execute trades based on predefined rules that create consistent, repeatable patterns on your chart.

ICT has reverse-engineered these algorithms by studying thousands of hours of price action across multiple markets and timeframes. The result is a trading methodology that identifies exactly where these algorithms are programmed to execute.

When you learn ICT, you are learning a lens for liquidity, imbalance and time; no published source code for markets exists. This algorithmic understanding is what separates ICT from every other trading methodology.

A dealing range is the price zone within which institutions accumulate or distribute their positions before a major move. In ICT, the dealing range is defined by a high and low boundary that contains price for an extended period.

Within this range, institutions build their positions slowly by buying near the low and selling near the high, or vice versa. The dealing range is always followed by an expansion move that breaks out of the range in the direction of institutional interest.

Identifying the dealing range on your chart allows you to position yourself ahead of the breakout. The larger the dealing range and the longer price spends within it, the more powerful the eventual breakout move will be.

Traditional market maker models assume that a single entity controls price, but ICT model recognizes that multiple institutions interact to create the market we see. The institutional model in ICT consists of three phases: accumulation, manipulation, and distribution.

This cycle repeats on every timeframe, from the 1-minute chart to the monthly chart. The same pattern that plays out over a week on the daily chart also plays out over minutes on the 1-minute chart. Understanding this fractal nature of the market is key to mastering ICT.
The institutional model is the lens through which you will view every chart from now on.

The Judas Swing is the term ICT uses for the manipulation phase of the institutional cycle. It is a sharp, seemingly aggressive move in one direction that traps retail traders before reversing violently in the true direction.
The Judas Swing gets its name from the biblical figure who betrayed with a kiss; the market appears to give you a profitable opportunity, only to reverse and take your money.

Recognizing the Judas Swing is essential because it is the moment when retail traders get trapped and institutional traders get positioned. If you can identify the Judas Swing in real time, you can avoid being the liquidity and instead ride the institutional move.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Practice exercise: Open a 1-hour chart of EUR/USD and scroll back 72 hours. Identify the most obvious dealing range, a period where price oscillated between a clear high and low for at least 12 hours. Mark the high and low with horizontal lines. Now look for the breakout from this range. Was it preceded by a sharp spike beyond one boundary, which is the Judas Swing, followed by a reversal through the range in the opposite direction? If so, you have identified the full institutional cycle: accumulation within the range, manipulation via the spike, and distribution through the breakout. Practice this on different pairs and timeframes until you can spot it instantly.

Institutions think in terms of risk management, liquidity, and time horizon. A large bank does not care about catching the exact top or bottom; they care about executing massive orders with minimal slippage. They plan their trades days or weeks in advance and execute according to algorithmic schedules.

Retail traders think in terms of quick profits, trading on impulse based on what price just did. This difference in time horizon and planning is why institutions consistently profit while retail traders consistently lose.
To trade like an institution, you must adopt their patience, their planning process, and their focus on risk management above all else.

Markets alternate between expansion and contraction phases. Contraction, also called consolidation or range-bound, is when price moves sideways within a dealing range, building liquidity. Expansion is when price breaks out of the range and trends strongly in one direction.

ICT teaches that you should trade during expansion and wait during contraction. Most retail traders do the opposite; they get bored during contraction and trade the noise, then get scared during expansion and miss the trend.

By identifying whether the market is in expansion or contraction, you can adjust your strategy accordingly. The contraction phase is for preparation and analysis; the expansion phase is for execution.

Illustrative example (not a real trade record): Consider EUR/USD in March 2024: price traded in a 50-pip dealing range between 1.0800 and 1.0850 for three full days. On the fourth day, price spiked down to 1.0790, the Judas Swing, grabbing stops below the range, then reversed and broke above 1.0850

within two hours. The breakout from the dealing range reached 1.0950 over the next 48 hours, a 100-pip move. Institutions accumulated long positions within the 1.0800-1.0850 range, manipulated stops below the range, and then distributed into the rally above 1.0950. This is the institutional cycle in action.
Had you identified the dealing range on day one, you would have been prepared for the breakout when the Judas Swing appeared.

lessons.title: Premium & Discount Arrays (PD Array)
lessons.subtitle: Identifying Institutional Buying and Selling Zones

steps.text: The Premium and Discount Array is the fundamental framework in ICT for determining where price is cheap and where it is expensive. It divides any price move into two halves using the 50% retracement level as the equilibrium.

The area below 50% is the discount zone, where institutions prefer to buy. The area above 50% is the premium zone, where institutions prefer to sell. The PD Array is not a single concept but a collection of tools including Fibonacci retracements, the 50% level, and the OTE zone that
work together to identify high-probability entry points. Understanding the PD Array is the prerequisite for every other ICT concept you will learn.

The premium zone is the upper half of any significant price swing, ranging from the 50% retracement level to the 100% level at the swing high. Price in the premium zone is considered expensive from an institutional perspective.

Institutions look to sell into the premium zone, especially when price reaches the 70.5% to 88.6% retracement area within it. Retail traders typically buy in the premium zone because they see price going up and want to join the move; this is exactly when institutions are distributing their long positions.
The premium zone is a warning sign for longs and an opportunity for shorts. Always be cautious when buying in premium territory.

The discount zone is the lower half of a price swing, ranging from the 0% level at the swing low to the 50% retracement level. Price in the discount zone is considered cheap from an institutional perspective.

Institutions look to buy in the discount zone, especially near the 61.8% to 78.6% retracement area when price comes into this zone from above. Retail traders typically sell in the discount zone because they see price falling and panic; this is exactly when institutions are accumulating long positions.
The discount zone is an opportunity for longs and a warning sign for shorts. The deeper the discount, the more attractive the price becomes for institutional buying.

The 50% retracement level is the equilibrium point in the PD Array. It represents fair value; the price level where neither buyers nor sellers have a clear advantage. Above 50%, the market is in premium territory; below 50%, the market is in discount territory.

The 50% level often acts as a magnet for price, meaning price tends to return to this level after significant moves. In ICT, the 50% level is one of the most important levels on your chart because it is the dividing line between institutional buying and selling zones.
When price crosses from discount to premium or vice versa, it signals a potential shift in market sentiment.

To draw the PD Array correctly, you must use structural swing points on your chart. For a bullish setup where you are looking to buy, identify a clear downward swing from a Higher High to a Lower Low.
Apply the Fibonacci retracement tool from the swing high at 100% to the swing low at 0%. The discount zone is from 0% to 50%, and the premium zone is from 50% to 100%.

For a bearish setup where you are looking to sell, identify a clear upward swing from a Higher Low to a Higher High. Apply Fibonacci from the swing low at 0% to the swing high at 100%. Always use structure-based swing points, not arbitrary highs and lows.

The PD Array becomes significantly more powerful when combined with market structure analysis. Do not trade PD Array levels in isolation; always filter them through the lens of higher timeframe structure.

If the daily chart is in an uptrend, you should only take buy setups in the discount zone of the 4-hour or 1-hour chart. If the daily chart is in a downtrend, only take sell setups in the premium zone on the lower timeframe.

When the higher timeframe structure aligns with the PD Array zone from the lower timeframe, you have a high-probability directional bias. Structure determines direction; PD Array determines the entry level.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Exercise: On a 4-hour EUR/USD chart, identify the most recent significant swing from a low to a high. Draw Fibonacci from the swing low to the swing high. Mark 0-50% as discount in green and 50-100% as premium in red. Now look at where price is currently trading. Based on the daily trend, should you be looking for buy entries or sell entries? If price is in discount and the daily trend is up, mark potential buy zones. If price is in premium and the daily trend is down, mark potential sell zones. This exercise trains you to align PD Array with structure before ever considering an entry.
Illustrative example (not a real trade record): Consider GBP/USD on the 4-hour chart in early 2024. Price made a swing high at 1.2800 and a swing low at 1.2600, a full 200-pip swing.

Fibonacci drawn from 1.2800 to 1.2600 showed the discount zone from 1.2600 to 1.2700 and the premium zone from 1.2700 to 1.2800. The daily chart was in a clear uptrend. Price pulled back into the premium zone at 1.2750 and formed a bearish Order Block.

A smart ICT trader would skip the short setup in premium because the daily trend was up. Price eventually broke above 1.2800 and rallied to 1.3000. This shows that higher timeframe structure always takes priority.

Common PD Array mistakes include drawing Fibonacci on the wrong swing points, using the PD Array without considering higher timeframe structure, entering at the 50% level without confirmation, and confusing premium for discount zones on different trend directions.
Another major mistake is expecting price to reverse exactly at the 50% level every time. The 50% level is a zone, not an exact line, and price may overshoot it slightly before reversing.
Always wait for confirmation such as a reversal candlestick pattern or an Order Block within your PD Array zone. The PD Array tells you where to look, not when to enter.

Master traders analyze the PD Array across multiple timeframes. Start with the weekly chart to identify the macro discount and premium zones. Move to the daily chart to refine within the weekly zones. Then use the 4-hour and 1-hour charts to find your entry within the daily zones.

The rule of thumb is: buy in the discount zone of the higher timeframe and look for the discount zone of the lower timeframe within that. If the weekly is in discount and the daily pulls back to its discount zone, that is a high-probability buy area.
Aligning PD Arrays across multiple timeframes gives you the highest probability setups in ICT.

lessons.title: Market Structure & Liquidity in ICT
lessons.subtitle: Advanced Structure, Displacement, and Market Structure Shifts

steps.text: Market structure in ICT goes beyond simple Higher Highs and Lower Lows. ICT introduces the concept of internal and external structure to provide a deeper understanding of price movements. External structure refers to the overall trend direction on the higher timeframe, while internal structure refers to the smaller swings within

that trend. A market structure shift occurs when internal structure breaks in the opposite direction of external structure, warning of a potential trend change. Understanding this layered structure allows you to identify when a pullback is just a pullback versus when it is the beginning of a reversal.

A displacement in ICT is a strong, aggressive candlestick or series of candles that breaks through a structural level with momentum. Displacement is characterized by a large body, small wicks, and a clear break beyond a key level.

This is distinct from a gradual move which lacks the institutional force behind it. A displacement tells you that institutions have committed to the direction with significant order flow. When you see a displacement, it confirms that the move is institutional and not random noise.
Always pay attention to displacement candles as they mark the points of highest institutional interest.

Liquidity voids are zones on the chart where price moved quickly without leaving overlapping candles, creating an area of thin trading. These voids occur when institutions push price aggressively through multiple price levels in a short period, leaving behind an area where few orders were filled.

Liquidity voids act as magnets for future price movement because the unfilled orders in that zone need to be satisfied. ICT teaches that price will often return to fill these voids before continuing in the original direction.
Identifying liquidity voids gives you both a target for profit-taking and a potential entry zone on retracement.

Internal structure refers to the smaller swings within the larger external trend. In an external uptrend, the internal structure consists of smaller Higher Highs and Higher Lows that make up the larger move.

A break of internal structure, where price breaks below a recent internal Higher Low, is the first warning sign that the external trend may be weakening. ICT traders watch for breaks of internal structure as early entry signals even before the external structure changes.
Trading with internal structure allows you to enter trends earlier and with tighter stop-losses compared to waiting for external structure breaks.

External structure is the dominant trend on the higher timeframe, typically the daily or weekly chart. It is defined by the sequence of major swing highs and swing lows. For an external uptrend, we see Higher Highs and Higher Lows on the daily chart.

For an external downtrend, we see Lower Highs and Lower Lows. The external structure determines your overall bias for the day or week. All lower timeframe trades should be taken in the direction of the external structure.
Fighting the external structure is the fastest way to lose money because you are trading against the institutional flow.

A Market Structure Shift, also called MSS in ICT, occurs when the internal structure breaks in the opposite direction of the external trend, signaling a potential reversal. For example, in an external uptrend, an MSS occurs when price breaks below the most recent Higher Low and forms a Lower Low.

This is the ICT equivalent of a Change of Character from SMC. The difference is that in ICT, an MSS is specifically tied to the displacement and liquidity concepts. A valid MSS is confirmed by three factors: a displacement through the structural level, a liquidity grab preceding the move, and
follow-through in the new direction.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Exercise: On a 1-hour chart of XAU/USD, identify the external structure using the daily chart; is it uptrend, downtrend, or ranging? Now identify the internal structure on the 1-hour chart. Mark the internal swing highs and lows. Look for any instance where internal structure broke in the opposite direction of the external trend. That is a potential MSS. Was it preceded by a liquidity grab at a key level? Was the break a displacement with a large candle? If yes, you have identified a high-probability MSS. Practice finding MSS on at least three different charts before your next trading session.

Liquidity sweeps occur when price briefly breaks beyond a key structural level to trigger stop-losses, then immediately reverses. In ICT, a liquidity sweep is the precursor to every significant reversal. The sweep confirms that institutions are active at that level and have collected the liquidity they need.

Without a liquidity sweep, a reversal is less reliable because there may not be enough fuel for the move. Always look for a sweep of the previous high before a short entry and a sweep of the previous low before a long entry.
The sweep validates that institutions are committed to the move.

Structure-based bias determination is a systematic process. Step 1: Check the daily chart external structure. Step 2: Identify any recent MSS or CHoCH that would change the daily bias. Step 3: On the 4-hour chart, identify the internal structure and liquidity levels.

Step 4: On the 1-hour chart, look for potential sweeps and displacement patterns. Step 5: Combine all this information into a single bias; bullish, bearish, or neutral. Your bias should never be based on a single timeframe or a single concept.
The more confluence you have across timeframes, the stronger your bias should be.

Combining structure with PD Array creates the complete ICT analytical framework. The structure tells you the direction, and the PD Array tells you the zone. Structure says buy or sell; PD Array says where to buy or sell.

For a long trade, you need: external uptrend confirmed, internal structure showing Higher Lows, price in the discount zone of the 4-hour PD Array. For a short trade, you need: external downtrend confirmed, internal structure showing Lower Highs, price in the premium zone of the 4-hour PD Array.
When structure and PD Array align perfectly, you have identified the ideal conditions for an institutional-grade trade setup.

lessons.title: Killzones — Institutional Execution Times
lessons.subtitle: London Open, NY Open, Asian Range, and London Close

steps.text: Killzones are ET windows when institutional flow is heaviest. One table (ET): Asian 8pm-12am range-building; London 2-5am breakout; New York 7-10am classic 7-9am trend and overlap; London Close 10am-12pm reversal and exits. Trade inside killzones; moves outside them are less reliable. Note: GMT offsets shift an hour in summer/winter with DST, always anchor to ET.

London Open Killzone LOKZ runs 2:00-5:00 AM ET. London brings massive orders, high volatility and large candles, often setting the day tone. Expect a liquidity grab in the first hour then a directional move. Be at the desk before 2:00 AM ET prepared with Asian high/low and PD Array. LOKZ moves are often the cleanest of the day.

New York Open Killzone NYOKZ runs 7:00-10:00 AM ET, classic 7-9am core. It overlaps London for deep liquidity and is the most volatile window. NY often confirms or reverses the London direction. If London rallied and NY continues, trend confirms. If NY reverses London, sentiment may be shifting. Plan both paths before 7:00 AM ET.

Asian window 8pm-12am ET is a killzone for range-building, not dead time. It typically forms a low-volatility range whose high and low become London breakout references. Break above the Asian high is bullish, below the low is bearish. Asian extremes are liquidity for London to target. Map the range before London; do not trade Asia noise without a plan.

London Close runs 10:00 AM-12:00 PM ET. As London desks close, profit-taking creates sharp reversals or accelerations into the New York direction. It is prime for entries with NY momentum. Expect fast wicks on exits. Note: GMT offsets shift an hour in summer/winter with DST, so confirm 10am-12pm ET on your chart, not GMT.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Exercise: Mark the killzones on your chart using vertical lines. Set your chart timezone to Eastern Standard Time. Draw a vertical line at 2:00 AM, 5:00 AM, 7:00 AM, 10:00 AM, and 11:00 AM EST. Now look back at the last week of data on EUR/USD. Observe how price behaves within each marked zone. You will notice that the majority of significant moves start within these killzone windows. Moves that start outside killzones are less reliable and more likely to reverse. This exercise will train your eye to see the market rhythm and help you understand why time is as important as price in ICT.

Trading each killzone requires a different strategy. For LOKZ, focus on breaks of the Asian range high or low with a confirmation candle. For NYOKZ, look for continuations or reversals of the London direction, using the PD Array from the 4-hour chart.

For London Close, look for sharp reversals as London traders exit positions. The common thread across all killzones is that you must have your bias and levels prepared before the killzone begins. Do not analyze during the killzone; analyze before it starts and execute when the conditions line up.
Preparation is the key to killzone trading.

The London/NY overlap from 7:00 AM to 12:00 PM EST is the most powerful trading period of the day. During this overlap, the full force of both European and American institutional order flow hits the market simultaneously. This is when you see the largest candlesticks and the most decisive breakouts.

ICT teaches that the overlap is the premier time for executing high-probability trades. The combination of the PD Array established during London, the liquidity grabbed during NY Open, and the volume from both sessions creates ideal conditions for the Power of 3 cycle to complete.

Combining killzones with the PD Array is where ICT really shines. Before each killzone, identify where price is trading relative to the PD Array on the 1-hour and 4-hour charts. If price is in the discount zone before LOKZ and the daily trend is up, prepare for a potential buy

setup during the London Open. If price is in the premium zone before NYOKZ and the daily trend is down, prepare for a sell setup. The killzone provides the timing, and the PD Array provides the level.
When both align, you have a complete ICT trade setup with a high probability of success.

Illustrative example (not a real trade record): Consider a real example: EUR/USD on a Tuesday in February 2024. The Asian range was 1.0750 to 1.0780. Price was in the discount zone of the 4-hour PD Array, and the daily trend was up.

At 2:15 AM EST, during LOKZ, price broke above the Asian high at 1.0780 and retested it as support. A trader prepared for this setup would have entered long at 1.0785 with a stop below the Asian low at 1.0745, targeting the next liquidity zone at 1.0850.
Price reached 1.0850 by 9:00 AM EST during NYOKZ, a 65-pip move with a risk-reward ratio of over 7:1. This is killzone trading at its finest.

steps.text: The Power of 3, also called PO3, is the core cycle that drives all price movement in ICT. PO3 stands for Accumulation, Manipulation, and Distribution. Accumulation is when institutions build their positions slowly, typically within a dealing range.

Manipulation is when they spike price in the opposite direction to grab liquidity and trap retail traders. Distribution is when they push price in the true direction to exit their positions at a profit. This three-phase cycle repeats continuously across all timeframes and all markets.
Understanding PO3 is understanding the heartbeat of the market.

The Accumulation phase is characterized by range-bound price action with low volatility. Price oscillates between a support and resistance level, creating a dealing range. During this phase, institutions are building their positions by buying near support and selling near resistance.

The accumulation phase can last from hours to days depending on the timeframe. Retail traders get bored during accumulation and often close their positions prematurely, handing their shares to institutions. The key to surviving accumulation is patience; your job is to identify the range and wait for the manipulation phase
to reveal the direction.

The Manipulation phase is the Judas Swing, a sharp break beyond the accumulation range in the opposite direction of the true move. This is the trap. Price spikes beyond the range boundary, triggering stop-losses and enticing traders to enter in the wrong direction.

The manipulation is designed to create maximum pain for retail traders. Immediately after grabbing liquidity, price reverses and breaks back into the range. The manipulation phase is short and violent, often lasting only one to three candles on the execution timeframe.
Recognizing this phase is the most important skill in PO3 trading.

The Distribution phase is the true directional move. After the manipulation spike and reversal, price breaks out of the accumulation range in the true direction and trends strongly. During distribution, institutions are exiting the positions they built during accumulation at a profit.

The distribution phase is characterized by strong momentum, large candlesticks, and often forms a Fair Value Gap. This is where you make your money as an ICT trader. The distribution phase continues until it reaches the next liquidity zone, where the cycle begins again.
Ride the distribution phase with confidence, knowing institutions are driving price.

The AMD cycle of Accumulation, Manipulation, Distribution can be visualized on any timeframe. On the 1-minute chart, it might complete in 15 minutes. On the daily chart, it might take two weeks. The cycle is fractal, meaning the same pattern repeats at every scale.

An AMD cycle on the daily chart consists of smaller AMD cycles on the 4-hour chart, which themselves consist of even smaller cycles on the 15-minute chart. Understanding this fractal nature allows you to zoom in for entries and zoom out for context.
The direction of the higher timeframe cycle dictates the direction you should trade on lower timeframes.

Multi-timeframe PO3 analysis is essential for proper trade execution. Start with the weekly chart: identify the current phase of the PO3 cycle. Is it accumulating, being manipulated, or distributing? Move to the daily chart: find the same cycle within the weekly phase. Then drop to the 4-hour for your entry.

For example, if the weekly is in distribution (trending up), the daily should be in accumulation or manipulation within that up-cycle. You want to enter at the end of the daily manipulation, which would align with the 4-hour discount zone.
This layered analysis ensures you are trading with multiple timeframe confluence.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Exercise: On a 1-hour chart of GBP/USD covering the last 48 hours, identify the three phases of PO3. Start by finding a clear range where price oscillated between two levels for several hours; that is accumulation. Now look for a spike beyond one boundary of the range followed by an immediate reversal; that is manipulation. Finally, find the breakout in the opposite direction of the spike that trends away from the range; that is distribution. Label each phase on your chart. Once you can spot all three phases clearly, try predicting what phase comes next from any point on the chart.

Combining PO3 with killzones creates a powerful timing mechanism. The accumulation phase often develops during the Asian session or during low-volatility periods. The manipulation phase frequently occurs at the London Open, as institutions use the influx of orders to grab liquidity.

The distribution phase then plays out during the NY session or London Close. By aligning the PO3 cycle with killzones, you can anticipate when each phase is likely to occur. For example, if you see accumulation during the Asian session, prepare for manipulation at the London Open and distribution during
the NY Open. This time-based anticipation is unique to ICT.

Illustrative example (not a real trade record): XAU/USD on a Wednesday in March 2024. Price accumulated between $2,150 and $2,170 for six hours during the Asian session. At 3:00 AM EST during LOKZ, price spiked down to $2,145, grabbing stops below the range; the manipulation.

Within 30 minutes, price reversed and broke above $2,170, then rallied to $2,200 by 9:00 AM EST during NYOKZ; the distribution. The full PO3 cycle completed in about 12 hours. A trader who recognized the accumulation phase during Asia would have been prepared for the manipulation at London Open and
could have entered long at the retest of $2,170 for a $30 move.

PO3 invalidation is mechanical. A wick poke beyond the 100% sweep extreme that closes back inside is a sweep to hold. A body close beyond 100% invalidates the setup — exit immediately, do not double down or average. Stand aside until a fresh accumulation forms. Illustrative framework, not a guarantee.

lessons.title: Optimal Trade Entry & Fibonacci in ICT
lessons.subtitle: ICT Fibonacci Levels, OTE Zone, and Confluence Trading

steps.text: ICT focuses on deeper retracements than traditional 38.2%, 50% and 61.8%. The OTE zone is 62%-79% of the swing, with 70.5% Consequent Encroachment (CE) as the sweet spot. 62% is the shallow edge and 79% the deep edge. Traditional 78.6% sits nearby but is NOT the ICT sweet spot. 88.6% lies beyond the zone — treat taps there as a beyond-zone warning, not an entry.

62% marks the OTE open, 70.5% CE is where institutional limit interest concentrates, and 79% is the deep limit. Price often reacts at 70.5% when a Fair Value Gap and Order Block align there. Do not anchor entries to 88.6%; it is outside OTE and signals overextension. Wait for price to hold inside 62%-79% with confirmation rather than chasing beyond-zone pokes.

The Optimal Trade Entry zone is 62%-79%, sweet spot 70.5% CE. For longs it sits on a down-retracement inside an uptrend; for shorts on an up-retracement inside a downtrend. Entering near 70.5% with FVG plus OB gives the best risk-reward. Combine OTE with higher-timeframe bias and killzone timing; OTE alone is not a signal.

The triple confluence of FVG plus OB plus 62%-79% OTE creates the highest-probability entry in ICT. When a Fair Value Gap overlaps an Order Block inside 62%-79% near 70.5% CE, three concepts point to the same area. Do not enter OTE without at least one confluence, preferably both FVG and OB together.

Stop placement: place stops beyond the 100% sweep wick, not 5-10 pips below the OB. A wick poke beyond 100% that closes back inside is a sweep to hold. A body close beyond 100% invalidates the setup — exit immediately. Never anchor stops to the OB edge; obvious OB edges are where liquidity hunts run.

ICT uses three primary extension targets: 127.2%, 141.4% and 161.8% of the original swing. 127.2% is the minimum target and often reached first. 141.4% is the intermediate target for trends. 161.8% is the maximum for strong trends. Take partials at each level: 50% at 127.2%, 30% at 141.4%, 20% runner to 161.8%.

To draw Fibonacci in ICT style, find the structural swing aligned with bias. For longs, take the down-swing inside an uptrend. Apply Fibonacci with 0% at the swing low and 100% at the swing high. Mark 62%, 70.5% CE and 79%. Then check for OB or FVG inside 62%-79%.
For shorts, invert: 0% low to 100% high still, then mark the same zone on the up-retracement.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Practice exercise: on 1-hour EUR/USD with 4-hour uptrend, find a down-retracement swing. Draw Fibonacci 0% low to 100% high. Mark 62%, 70.5% CE and 79% (OTE 62%-79%). Look for Order Block plus Fair Value Gap inside the zone near 70.5%. Plan entry on confirmation, stop beyond the 100% sweep wick, targets at 127.2%, 141.4%, 161.8%. Body close beyond 100% invalidates.

Illustrative example (not a real trade record): USD/JPY 1-hour, 4-hour uptrend. Down-swing 151.50 to 150.00. OTE 62%-79% is about 150.93 to 151.19, sweet spot 70.5% CE near 151.06. Bullish Order Block plus FVG overlapped near 151.00-151.10. Entry on bullish confirmation near 151.06, stop beyond the 100% sweep wick; body close beyond 100% invalidates. Partial at 127.2% extension.

Common OTE mistakes: wrong swing, entering before 62%-79%, ignoring FVG/OB confluence, anchoring to 88.6% beyond the zone, placing stops at obvious OB edges, wrong extensions, exiting early. 88.6% is beyond-zone warning, not entry. 78.6% is nearby traditional fib, not the 70.5% CE sweet spot. Filter every OTE with structure and killzone timing.

lessons.title: Time & Price Theory
lessons.subtitle: ICT Specific Times, Time Cycles, and Price-Time Alignment

steps.text: Time and Price Theory: institutions execute in windows. Official ICT Silver Bullet windows (ET): 3-4am London, 10-11am New York morning, 2-3pm New York afternoon. A valid setup needs sweep plus market-structure shift plus FVG all INSIDE the window. 8:30am ET news invalidates models — stand aside and wait for post-news structure.

Silver Bullet 10-11am ET is the New York morning window. Watch for a liquidity sweep of the NY Open extreme, then a market-structure shift, then an FVG entry inside 10-11am. No trade without all three inside the window. If 8:30am ET news spiked volatility, skip the window until structure rebuilds.

Silver Bullet continuation develops inside the same 10-11am ET window after the first shift. Once sweep plus shift plus FVG align, distribution often extends through 11am. Do not chase outside the window. If price never sweeps or never shifts inside 10-11am, there is no Silver Bullet trade that day.

Silver Bullet 2-3pm ET is the afternoon window for end-of-day adjustment. Same rule: sweep plus shift plus FVG must occur INSIDE 2-3pm. Institutions reposition for the close. 8:30am news effects fade by afternoon, but fresh late headlines still invalidate. Trade only clean inside-window structure.

Silver Bullet 3-4am ET covers the London window. Same inside-window rule applies to the overnight sweep and shift. Time cycles help context: 4-hour, daily and weekly rhythms frame bias, but execution still needs sweep plus shift plus FVG inside one Silver Bullet window. No inside-window confluence means no trade.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Exercise: on 15-minute EUR/USD mark Silver Bullet windows 3-4am, 10-11am and 2-3pm ET for five days. For each window check: did a sweep plus MSS plus FVG all occur INSIDE the window? Only inside-window alignment counts. Note 8:30am ET news days as invalid. Track your own counts; do not use fixed reversal percentages.

Price-time alignment occurs when price reaches a key ICT level at the same time as a key ICT time event. This is the holy grail of ICT trading. For example, if price retraces to the 78.6% Fibonacci OTE zone exactly at 10:00 AM EST, and an Order Block exists at

that level, you have the perfect alignment of price, time, and structure. When price and time align, the probability of a reversal is at its highest. ICT teaches that you should prioritize trades where time and price align over trades where only price is aligned.
Time confirms that institutions are active at that moment.

Liquidity runs are movements that target specific liquidity pools with precise timing. ICT teaches that institutions time their liquidity runs to coincide with killzones and specific time events for maximum effectiveness. A liquidity run during a killzone has more power and follow-through than one occurring outside of trading hours.

For example, a sweep of the Asian high at 2:15 AM EST during LOKZ is more likely to lead to a sustained move than the same sweep happening at 6:00 AM EST during the London lunch break. Timing amplifies the effectiveness of liquidity runs significantly.

Forecasting with time and price is the ultimate ICT skill. To forecast, start with the time: which killzone is coming next, and what time events will occur during it? Then determine the price: where is the PD Array and OTE zone relative to current price?

If the next event is NYOKZ at 9:00 AM, and price is in the discount zone approaching an OTE level, you can forecast a potential reversal at 10:00 AM from that level. Write your forecast down before the event and compare it to what actually happens.
Forecasting trains your brain to think algorithmically and improves your pattern recognition over time.
Illustrative example (not a real trade record): Real example: On a Thursday in April 2024, GBP/USD was in a 4-hour uptrend. Price pulled back to the 78.6% OTE level at 1.2500 by 9:45 AM EST.

At exactly 10:00 AM EST, price formed a bullish engulfing candle at the OTE level, with an Order Block at 1.2490 and an FVG from 1.2490 to 1.2505. This was perfect price-time alignment: OTE plus OB plus FVG plus 10:00 AM reversal time.
Price reversed from 1.2500 and rallied to 1.2580 by 12:00 PM, an 80-pip move. A trader prepared for the 10:00 AM reversal would have caught the entire move with a tight stop below 1.2490.

lessons.title: Complete ICT Trading Plan
lessons.subtitle: 9-Step Plan from Analysis to Review with Full Worked Example

steps.text: Step 1: Determine your Higher Timeframe Bias. Start with the daily chart; identify whether the market is in an uptrend with Higher Highs and Higher Lows, a downtrend with Lower Highs and Lower Lows, or ranging. Then check the weekly chart for additional context.

Your bias for the day must match the daily and weekly structure. If the daily is in an uptrend, you are only looking for long trades. If it is in a downtrend, only short trades. If it is ranging, you wait for a structure break before committing.
This single step eliminates most losing trades because you stop fighting the institutional trend.

Step 2: Identify the PD Array and premium/discount zones. On the 4-hour chart, identify the most recent significant swing that aligns with your daily bias. Draw Fibonacci from the swing high to swing low.

Mark the discount zone from 0-50%, the premium zone from 50-100%, and the OTE zone from 62%-79% (sweet spot 70.5% CE; 88.6% is beyond-zone warning). Note where current price sits relative to these zones.
If you are bullish and price is in the discount zone, you have a potential buy zone. If you are bearish and price is in the premium zone, you have a potential sell zone.
If price is in the wrong zone for your bias, wait for it to move into the correct zone.

Step 3: Select the appropriate Killzone. Based on the current time, determine which killzone is active or approaching. If it is between 2 AM and 5 AM EST, you are in LOKZ. If between 7 AM and 10 AM EST, you are in NYOKZ.

If between 11 AM and 12 PM EST, you are in London Close. If you are outside killzone hours, do not trade; spend this time analyzing higher timeframes and preparing for the next killzone. The killzone provides the timing for your trade.
Even if price is at the perfect PD Array level, do not enter if you are outside a killzone unless the setup is exceptional.

Step 4: Anticipate the Power of 3 cycle. Determine which phase of PO3 the market is currently in. If price is ranging during the Asian session, you are in accumulation and should prepare for manipulation at the next killzone.

If price is spiking during LOKZ, you are likely in the manipulation phase and should wait for the reversal and distribution. If price is trending strongly during NYOKZ, you are in distribution and should look to ride the move.
Understanding where you are in the PO3 cycle helps you anticipate what comes next and positions you for the highest-probability entry.

Step 5: Identify Fair Value Gaps and Order Blocks. On the 15-minute or 1-hour chart, look for a Fair Value Gap created by the manipulation spike or the initial distribution move. Then find the Order Block; the last candle before the aggressive move that created the FVG.

Draw these zones on your chart. If the FVG and OB overlap with your OTE zone from Step 2, you have triple confluence. If only one is present, the setup is still valid but less reliable. If neither is present, skip the trade.
The FVG and OB are your confirmation that institutions participated in the move at that level.

Step 6: Define your OTE entry zone. On the lower timeframe, refine your entry to the specific price level within the OTE zone where the OB and FVG are located. Mark the exact entry price, the stop beyond the 100% sweep wick (body close beyond = invalid), and your three

extension targets at 127.2%, 141.4%, and 161.8%. Your entry should be a limit order placed at the OB level, not a market order chasing price. If price does not reach your OTE zone, do not force the trade. Missing a trade is better than taking a bad one.
The market will eventually give you another opportunity.

Step 7: Execute the trade with precision. Wait for price to enter your OTE zone and form a confirmation candle. For a long trade, the confirmation is a bullish reversal candle such as a hammer, bullish engulfing, or inside bar breakout to the upside.

For a short trade, it is a bearish reversal candle such as a shooting star, bearish engulfing, or inside bar breakout to the downside. Enter on the close of the confirmation candle. Do not enter before the candle closes, as the wick may trap you.
Once entered, set your stop and first target immediately.

Step 8: Manage the trade actively. Once price moves in your favor, take 50% profit at the 127.2% extension target and move your stop to breakeven. Let the remaining 50% run with a trailing stop behind each new structural level.

For a long trade, trail your stop below each new Higher Low. For a short trade, trail your stop above each new Lower High. Take an additional 25% profit at the 141.4% target and let the final 25% run to the 161.8% target with a wider stop.
If price reverses and hits your breakeven stop on the remaining position, the trade was still a winner overall.

Step 9: Review and journal the trade immediately. Write down: the daily bias, the PD Array zone, the killzone used, the PO3 phase, the FVG and OB levels, the entry and exit prices, the risk-reward ratio, the outcome, and your emotional state during the trade.

Did you follow every step of the plan? Did you exit early because of fear? Did you move your stop emotionally? A trading journal is the fastest way to improve. Review your journal weekly and identify patterns in your mistakes.
Most traders repeat the same errors until they write them down and consciously work to correct them.

Risk note: most retail traders lose money. Never risk more than 1–2% of your account on any single trade, practice on a demo account first, and remember that stop orders can slip on news and weekend gaps.

Practice on the ict_8_practice H1 chart (EUR/USD): mark the Asian-range liquidity box, then the manipulation sweep low, then the FVG and the bullish Order Block inside OTE 62%-79% near 70.5% CE. Plan entry on confirmation with stop beyond the 100% sweep wick. Body close beyond 100% invalidates. Log bias, killzone, PO3 phase and risk (max 1-2%, max 3 trades/day).

Risk is non-negotiable. CFDs and leveraged FX carry high risk; most retail traders lose money. Stops are not guaranteed and can slip on news and weekend gaps. Never risk more than 1-2% per trade, max 3 trades per day, practice on demo first. 8:30am ET news invalidates ICT models — do not trade into it. Trust a disciplined process, not profit targets.
